query: Consider the following context: Refractory high-entropy alloys (HEAs) are promising candidates for next-generation nuclear applications, particularly fusion reactors, due to their excellent high-temperature mechanical properties and irradiation resistance. In that context, which material can be used for low-activation structural material for high-temperature plasma-facing components (PFCs) in fusion reactors, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Refractory high-entropy alloys (HEAs) formulated entirely from low‐activation elements can serve as effective structural materials for high-temperature plasma‐facing components in fusion reactors by offering superior irradiation resistance and reduced helium-induced degradation compared to tungsten.
generation.material_initial_state: An as-cast or homogenized refractory HEA composed of low-activation elements (e.g., a tailored composition excluding elements that produce long-lived radioactive isotopes)
generation.intervention: Expose the HEA to simulated fusion reactor conditions including high temperatures (≥1000 K), high fluxes of helium ions, and neutron irradiation
generation.conditions: Laboratory irradiation experiments and high-temperature mechanical tests mimicking plasma-facing reactor conditions (thermal cycling, high heat flux, and particle bombardment)
generation.structural_mediator: The complex, multi-element microstructure of the HEA, which promotes sluggish diffusion and enhanced defect recombination that suppresses the formation and coalescence of irradiation-induced helium bubbles
generation.mechanism: The distributed lattice distortion inherent in HEAs reduces the mobility of defects created during irradiation, mitigating helium bubble growth and embrittlement while maintaining high-temperature mechanical strength, unlike tungsten that suffers from helium bubble formation and embrittlement
generation.predicted_outcome: Under fusion-relevant conditions, the HEA is expected to exhibit lower helium-induced damage, superior high-temperature mechanical stability, and reduced activation (due to selection of low-activation constituent elements) when compared to conventional tungsten-based plasma-facing components
generation.baseline: Current tungsten-based materials used in plasma-facing components, which have high melting points but suffer from helium bubble formation and brittleness under irradiation
generation.boundary: The hypothesis may not hold if the selected low-activation elements in the HEA inadvertently lead to unstable phases or if unforeseen activation products arise; additionally, long-term performance under continuous fusion conditions remains to be validated
generation.uncertainty: The magnitude of the performance improvements (e.g., reductions in helium bubble density and improvements in high-temperature mechanical properties) is uncertain without direct experimental data, and the optimal composition window for low activation versus mechanical performance requires further investigation

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare samples of the designed low-activation refractory HEA and benchmark tungsten samples. Subject both sets to high-temperature (≥1000 K) and high-dose irradiation tests that simulate plasma-facing conditions, including exposure to helium ions and neutrons. Conduct thermal cycling and mechanical tests (e.g., high-temperature tensile and creep tests) post-irradiation.
measurements: Helium bubble density and size (via SEM/TEM)
High-temperature tensile strength and fracture toughness
Activation levels using gamma spectroscopy post-irradiation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the refractory HEA exhibits either higher helium bubble formation or inferior high-temperature mechanical performance and activation levels that are not lower compared to tungsten under identical test conditions, the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Clean energy production is the cornerstone of our time. Options for sustainable clean energy include advanced power generation systems that have the potential to drastically reduce the emission of greenhouse gases. These advanced systems are often required to operate under harsh conditions to optimize efficiency, which poses several challenges for the available materials. An example of advanced power system is one that is associated with fusion energy [1] . Beyond traditional fission-based systems, fusion reactors not only promise nearly unlimited clean energy, but also avoid the generation of long-life radioactive waste produced in fission devices. One remaining challenge is that of materials, which can withstand extreme conditions of radiation, temperature, and stress, with long-term steady properties for the power plant to be economically viable [2] – [4] . A key component in current tokamak designs is the divertor, which will be in contact with the deuterium-tritium (D-T) plasma and sustain severe fluxes of particles (helium (He) ash, D and T) and heat, along with radiation damage induced by high-energy neutrons [2] , [3] . The present work discovers the unique deformation behavior of a refractory high-entropy alloy at elevated temperatures.

Key components in magnetic fusion reactors, such as the divertor or the plasma-facing materials (PFMs), are required to have stringent properties including low activation, high melting point, good thermomechanical properties, low sputter erosion, and low tritium retention/codeposition. They must operate at high temperature (≥1000 K) for long durations (>10 7 s), without failure or extensive erosion while exposed to large plasma heat and an intense mixture of ionized and energetic neutral species of hydrogen isotopes (D and T), He ash (fluxes, >10 24 m −2 s −1 ), and neutrons ( [1] ). Tungsten (W) is the leading PFM candidate because of its high melting temperature, low erosion rates, and small tritium retention. These advantages are unfortunately coupled with very low fracture toughness characterized by brittle transgranular and intergranular failure regimes, which severely restrict the useful operating temperature window and also create a range of fabrication difficulties. Furthermore, blistering at moderate temperature (<800 K) by D and He ( [2] , [3] ) and the formation of pits, holes, and bubbles by He at higher temperature (>1600 K) ( [4] ) have all been observed.
